meta.name: Hyperemesis with Dehydration — Straightforward IV Access

patient.name: Emily Carter
patient.chiefComplaint: Nausea and vomiting for 3 days, now weak and dizzy

history.hpi: Patient reports three days of persistent nausea and vomiting, unable to keep down food or most liquids. Today she felt lightheaded and nearly fainted getting out of bed, prompting her husband to call EMS. She is 8 weeks pregnant by her last menstrual period and was told by her OB last week this could be hyperemesis gravidarum. Denies abdominal pain, fever, or vaginal bleeding.
pastMedical: Hyperemesis gravidarum, suspected (per OB, last week)
history.lastOralIntake: A few sips of water 1 hour ago; last solid food tolerated was 2 days ago
history.events: Husband called 911 after patient became lightheaded and nearly fainted standing up

scene.dispatch: 24-year-old female, nausea and vomiting, weakness, residence
scene.location: Second-floor apartment bedroom, patient lying on bed
scene.bystanders: Husband present, called 911 and has been assisting patient to the bathroom
visualCues: Emesis basin on nightstand with recent contents
Several empty water bottles, mostly untouched
Patient pale, lying still on the bed with eyes closed
Blanket pulled up despite warm room

phases.name: Initial Contact
phases.description: Crew arrives to find a 24-year-old female, 8 weeks pregnant, pale and fatigued in bed after three days of vomiting. She is alert but reports dizziness when sitting up and has not tolerated oral intake.

clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses present, rapid and thready
otherFindings: Reports dizziness and near-syncope when standing
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "I just can't keep anything down. I felt like I was going to pass out getting up."

transitions.if: IV access obtained, NS bolus started
transitions.condition: Crew establishes a forearm IV without difficulty, checks blood glucose, and initiates a normal saline bolus per the Shock guideline.

transitions.if: IV access delayed, no fluids given
transitions.condition: Crew delays IV attempts or defers fluid administration, allowing ongoing volume loss from vomiting to progress toward uncompensated shock.

phases.name: IV access obtained, NS bolus started
phases.description: Crew establishes forearm IV access, checks blood glucose, administers ondansetron for nausea, and begins a normal saline bolus targeting improved perfusion.
phases.triggerCondition: After the crew performs a straightforward forearm IV stick, checks glucose, and initiates a normal saline bolus per the Shock guideline along with an antiemetic for ongoing nausea.

otherFindings: 18ga IV in place, right forearm, flushing well

expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Establish IV access. If unable to obtain within two attempts or less than 90 seconds, place an IO needle
expectedActions.rationale: Vascular access is required for fluid resuscitation and antiemetic administration.
Rules out hypoglycemia as a contributor to weakness and dizziness.

expectedActions.shortAction: Normal saline 500 mL IV bolus, pressure infused over <15 min
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: IV fluid volume goal attained by giving boluses that are pressure infused over less than 15 minutes each based on patient's condition and clinical impression... Fluid goal of up to 30 mL/kg of isotonic fluid by administering rapid, predetermined boluses (e.g., 500 mL) unless the MAP goal is achieved, or pulmonary edema develops
expectedActions.rationale: Restores intravascular volume lost from several days of emesis and poor intake.

expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Ondansetron (contraindicated for suspected or known diagnosis of prolonged QT syndrome) Adult: 4 mg IV/PO/SL
expectedActions.rationale: Controls ongoing nausea/vomiting to prevent further fluid losses.

transitions.condition: Heart rate trends down, blood pressure improves, and nausea subsides after the bolus and antiemetic; patient is packaged for transport.

phases.name: Improved with fluids and ondansetron
phases.description: Patient's tachycardia and hypotension improve after the fluid bolus and antiemetic. She is reassessed serially and transported to an appropriate facility for OB evaluation.
phases.triggerCondition: After the initial 500 mL bolus and ondansetron, the patient's perfusion and nausea improve, and the crew prepares her for transport with ongoing reassessment.

clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "I feel a lot less dizzy now, thank you."

expectedActions.shortAction: Reassess vital signs serially en route; monitor for recurrent nausea
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Full vital signs (pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate, neurologic status assessment) with reassessment q 15 minutes or more frequently as appropriate
expectedActions.rationale: Confirms sustained improvement and catches early recurrence of symptoms.

phases.name: IV access delayed, no fluids given
phases.description: Without IV access or fluid resuscitation, ongoing volume loss from vomiting drives the patient toward uncompensated shock, with worsening tachycardia and new hypotension.
phases.triggerCondition: IV attempts are delayed or fluids are withheld, allowing continued volume depletion from vomiting; the patient's compensated shock progresses toward hypotension.

clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Strength intact but patient appears increasingly lethargic

expectedActions.shortAction: Recognize progression to uncompensated shock; establish IV/IO access emergently
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Hypotension indicates uncompensated shock, which may progress to cardiopulmonary failure within minutes... Establish IV access. If unable to obtain within two attempts or less than 90 seconds, place an IO needle
expectedActions.rationale: Delayed volume replacement allows compensated shock to progress to hypotension, a late and dangerous sign.
